newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: INTERVIEW - Portugal says will pass the EMU test.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Portugal says will pass the EMU test.

text.p: Portugal will pass the entry tests for monetary union and become a founder member of the single currency at its launch in 1999, deputy finance minister Fernando Teixeira dos Santos said.

He told Reuters that even the debt to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio, the one criteria that on paper Portugal has no chance of satisfying, should prove no problem in practice as the figure was declining and that was the key issue.
"I have absolutely no doubt that we will be in (monetary union," he said in an interview on Monday night.

Teixeira dos Santos, Secretary of State for the Treasury and Finance, said that Portugal was not a recent convert to the cause of financial discipline, having steadily cut back its budget deficit since the early 1990s.

Lisbon would also be able to sustain tight budgetary control, with an economic plan for the years 1998-2000, which is due to be presented to Portugal's European Union partners in March, forecasting a deficit of below two percent at the end of the period.
"This process of convergence is solid and sustainable," he said.

Suggestions that some aspiring members of monetary union, particularly southern European countries, are latecomers to the notion of financial discipline and so probably not able to sustain the effort, are often cited as reasons why these countries should not join in the first wave.

Financial markets, which had been betting heavily on Spain, Italy and Portugal joining Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at the start, began to have second thoughts late last week as speculation also swirled of a delay to the whole project.
But Teixeira dos Santos ruled out any postponement, saying that the political commitment of member countries to meeting the January 1, 1999 launch date for economic and monetary union was too strong.
"It makes no sense to speak of any other scenario," he said.
He said that Portugal was aware that it could expect no favours when European Union states met to decide in the spring of 1998 which countries had qualified.
Portugal would only get in if it satisfied the criteria, which include a three percent of GDP limit for the budget deficit and ceilings for inflation.
"Portugal will have to gain entry on its merits, by meeting the criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty (the EMU blueprint)," he said.

Echoing the optimism expressed last week by Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco, Teixeira dos Santos said that signs that the economy was growing faster than expected together with strong tax receipts suggested that the 1997 budget deficit could be lower than the 2.9 percent programmed.
The government, however, prefered to be cautious and for the time being would not be cutting its forecast.
"But if there are any changes, they will be for the better," Teixeira dos Santos said.
He noted that the debt-to-GDP ratio had fallen by more than one percentage point in 1996 and would fall by at least the same amount this year to around 69 percent.
Although this was above the 60 percent ceiling, the Maastricht Treaty spelt out that it was important that the ratio should be falling and on this basis, Portugal satisfied the requirement, he said.
"Our public debt will have a trend that is compatible with the Maastricht Treaty," he said.

The finance ministry official firmly dismissed attempts to lump Portugal together with Spain and Italy in a so-called 'Club Med' for the purpose of assessing prospects for southern European countries to join the single currency at the start.
Apart from the geographical inaccuracy of placing Portugal on the Mediterranean, Teixeira dos Santos said that the three countries had the right to be judged individually.
"Portugal cannot be grouped in some geographic bloc. It has its own identity and prospects," he said.
